subject: research/energy-store-flip
professional: a senior energy-systems techno-economic analyst (the kind who builds LCOH comparisons on the Danish Energy Agency / PyPSA technology-data catalogues and referees for Applied Energy or Energy). They would check first that costs and prices are on one currency-year basis, that the sensitivity moves inputs the way they actually co-move (a table vintage moves every row, not one), that uncertainty ranges come from the catalogue's own lower/upper columns, and that the heat-pump side (COP, full-load hours) is credible, since its capex dominates the house comparison

evidence.correctness: Every number in results.txt recomputes with an independent script (numpy, own parsing of energy-thermal-cost/data/params.csv, own capital-recovery-factor + FOM annualisation, own cheapest-quarter and November-March means from the price files' own timestamps, flip multipliers in closed form because the margin is linear in each capex multiplier; only the physical sizing size_for_delivery is borrowed). All 30 house/district daily/weekly/monthly diffs, x_store and x_hp agree to the printed digits (e.g. house weekly -0.0044/-0.0053/-0.0054/+0.0111/-0.0005, x_store 1.16/1.20/1.20/0.59/1.02, x_hp 0.93/0.91/0.91/1.18/0.99; monthly 2018 'none'). Vintage ratios 1.2573 (store, charger) and 1.2623 (both heat pumps) match README:28. A 200,000-draw numpy Monte Carlo reproduces section C/D within sampling error: weekly h=0.10 win shares 0.85/0.905/0.91/0.00/0.54 vs 0.84/0.90/0.90/0.00/0.53; sd_year 0.0063, sd_cost 0.0039 (h=0.10) and 0.0097 vs 0.0098 (h=0.25), year share 0.72/0.29; daily mean -0.0217. Hand check of the heat-pump capital part: 5 kW x 1135.43 EUR/kW x (CRF(4%,18)=0.0790 + 3.0014% FOM) / 10,000 kWh = 0.0619 EUR/kWh, as the script. Not 4: the numbers are right relative to the table, but sd_year uses the population (ddof=0) sd of five years (sample sd 0.0070) without saying so.
evidence.completeness: README promises: run.py reproduces results.txt in about 30 s (rerun: 31.3 s, `diff` byte-identical); 6 tests (6 passed in 1.15 s); sections A to D present with the stated grids (bisection 0.05 to 20, 1,000 draws seed 20261023, 500 draws for D); live page https://marisstella.app/research/energy-store-flip/ HTTP 200 with the summary numbers. Next steps are labelled as not done. Everything claimed as done runs end to end.
evidence.verification: `cd research/energy-store-flip && /usr/bin/python3.13 -m pytest tests -q`: 6 passed in 1.15 s. The base-case test pins the weekly house diffs to energy-thermal-real (abs 0.0006) and the flip test checks a zero of the margin, so changes to the cost path are caught (2 of 2: charger dropped from scaled; charge fraction 0.25 -> 0.5). The Monte Carlo and variance code are effectively untested: 3 of 3 seeded mutants survived via platform/ci/quality_mutate.py (within-year variance taken around the grand mean instead of the year mean, model.py:94; between-year variance divided by 25 instead of 5, model.py:93; win test `< 0` -> `< 0.001`, model.py:82). The variance test only asserts b > 0 and w > 0. Nothing pins results.txt or the README's section C/D numbers.
evidence.craft: Read src/energy_store_flip/model.py (95 lines), __init__.py, tests/test_model.py, experiments/run.py, and the imported energy_thermal_cost/cost.py and energy_thermal_hourly/prices.py. Small, clear, stdlib, deterministic. Defects: model.py:21 monkeypatches the sibling package's module global (`_cost.size_for_delivery = lru_cache(...)`) at import, a side effect on any other importer; model.py:13-16 mutates sys.path, so the pyproject package is not installable on its own; model.py:34 loads the price file twice; flip_multiplier runs 60 bisection steps (each a deepcopy of the whole table) on a function that is linear in the multiplier and has a closed form; win_share's default n=2000 differs from the 1,000 the README and run.py use. None changes a result.
evidence.claims: Checked against files and recomputation: all headline numbers (README:10-13, project.json summary/lede) are in results.txt and recompute. Problems: (1) README:10 'The table's own vintage step ... is 1.257 times for the store, so choosing the older or newer table alone flips the verdict in the four years where the store wins' compares a store-only 1.257x step with x_store, but the same vintage step moves the heat pump by 1.262x. Moving the whole table up a step never flips (house weekly diffs -0.0138/-0.0147/-0.0148/+0.0017/-0.0098: the store wins more). Moving to the real older table (v0.9.2) does flip all four (+0.0030/+0.0021/+0.0020/+0.0069), but because the heat pump gets cheaper, the opposite mechanism from the one stated. The project.json summary and live page repeat '(1.257x) alone flips four of five years'. (2) '2 to 40% change' when 0.59 is a 41% cut (low). (3) sd_year is a population sd over five years, unstated. Limitations are otherwise specific and candid (h assumed, HX not costed, capex only, wholesale).
evidence.fitness: Job: a researcher deciding whether energy-thermal-real's 'weekly cycling mostly favours the store' survives cost uncertainty, or extending the model. The tables do answer the narrow one-at-a-time question and the code is easy to extend. But the most relevant joint move is missed: scaling all capex together by less than 0.85 (house weekly; 0.986 for 2019) hands every year to the heat pump, and the 2025-EUR costs against 2015-2019 nominal prices make exactly such a move (about 0.8) the consistent comparison. The heat-pump capital part (0.062 EUR/kWh) is 2.3 times the store's (0.027), so the verdict is mainly a heat-pump capex question, which the README does not say. Nearest prior work: catalogue sensitivity practice (Danish Energy Agency Technology Data, lower/upper columns; PyPSA technology-data), sand/particle thermal storage techno-economics (e.g. Gifford et al. NREL particle TES; Polar Night Energy pilot), and LCOH comparisons of heat pumps and thermal storage; none cited. As research it is a sensitivity table on a repository-internal model, well short of the PhD bar the research track sets.
evidence.domain: Against standard techno-economic practice (real/nominal consistency, e.g. IEA/DEA LCOE methodology; joint or global sensitivity, Saltelli et al. 2008): (a) capex in 2025 euros (params.csv currency_year 2025 for head_2030) is compared with nominal 2015-2019 wholesale prices with no deflation; a ~0.80 joint deflator flips house weekly to the pump in all five years (auditor assumption for the deflator: German HICP roughly 2017 -> 2025, about +25%), and the README calls the vintage ratio 'inflation, not technical uncertainty' without drawing that consequence; (b) one-at-a-time multipliers for two inputs that move together under any table revision; (c) h assumed rather than from the catalogue's own ranges (disclosed); (d) variance split with five years and ddof=0; (e) constant COP 3.6 and 2000 full-load hours for an ASHP (disclosed as fixed). The arithmetic is sound; a practitioner would reject the framing of the vintage result and ask for a currency-consistent base case first.

verdict: Arithmetically right and fully reproducible, but its main interpretive claim rests on a one-sided reading of the cost table. run.py reproduces results.txt byte for byte in 31 s, 6 tests pass, and an independent numpy recomputation (own LCOH, own price reductions, closed-form flips, 200k-draw Monte Carlo) matches every flip multiplier, win share and variance figure. It misses the bar on claims, verification and domain: the README says the table's 1.257x vintage step flips the weekly verdict through the store's capex, when the same step moves the heat pump 1.262x (a whole-table step up flips nothing; the older table flips all four years through the cheaper pump). More fundamentally, 2025-euro costs are set against nominal 2015-2019 prices, and any joint capex scaling below 0.85 (about the inflation gap) hands weekly cycling to the heat pump in every year. 3 of 5 seeded mutants in the Monte Carlo and variance code survive, and no prior work is cited.
